source_read: PMC full text PMC4459504 (accepted author manuscript NIHMS692958) in the reader's own browser tab: abstract, all sections, Tables 1A, 1B, 2A and 2B (rendered as text, with notes), declaration of interests and references. Paragraph structure was checked in the page DOM (Discussion has 8 paragraphs). The supplement (Word file) was not opened, as the brief requires. Step 1 completed before the card was opened.

claims.overstatement: None for this source. The claim is more cautious than the authors, who write that their analyses 'support a causal effect' (Discussion, 7th paragraph). Given non-shared confounding, exposure measurement error and the null within-MZ result for abuse or dependence symptoms, that caution is warranted. Minor wording: (1) the within-pair estimates are a little over a third of the weighted estimate (0.21/0.57 = 0.37; MZ 0.22/0.57 = 0.39), so 'about a third' slightly understates them; (2) the '29 childhood characteristics' were measured at the age-11 intake: 9 describe the twin, 20 the family and parents (parental substance use, psychopathology, education, income and others).
claims.note: Every number from this source in the statement and magnitude was checked against Methods › Participants, Tables 1A and 2A/2B, and matches: born 1977-1984; 1512 at intake (mean age 11.72); exposure self-reported at the age-14 follow-up (mean 14.8); outcomes at FU4 (mean 25.29). Weighted 0.57 (0.06); all pairs 0.21 (0.09); MZ 0.22 (0.10); DZ 0.20 (0.14). Abuse or dependence symptoms: weighted 0.36; all pairs 0.24 (0.11); MZ 0.17 (0.14); DZ 0.34 (0.16). Intoxication, all pairs 0.29 (0.15). 'Already differed beforehand, notably in delinquent behaviour and parents' drinking and smoking' matches Table 1A (standardized differences 0.51, 0.39 and 0.45; 13 of 29 covariates above 0.25). Editors' calculations from beta and SE (two-sided normal): all pairs p about 0.020, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.39; MZ p about 0.028, CI 0.02 to 0.42; MZ abuse or dependence symptoms p about 0.22, CI -0.10 to 0.44; intoxication all pairs p about 0.053. 'Remained' and 'not clearly associated' therefore hold without the printed p-values, which are not valid (see the p-value anchor). The caveat sentence is supported by the Discussion, 6th paragraph, and the co-twin Methods paragraph. Its example ('their own early use of tobacco or other drugs') is the editors' illustration, not the paper's, but it fits the paper: none of the 29 propensity covariates measures the twins' own substance use (Table 1A). Qualifiers the claim leaves out: zygosity did not significantly moderate any within-pair effect (Results › Estimated Effects, 2nd paragraph); the authors note that random exposure measurement error also shrinks within-pair estimates (Discussion, 4th paragraph); the exposure is 'by FU1' at mean age 14.8, not strictly by 14.

anchors.extracted: Minnesota Twin Family Study, population-based (called community-based in the abstract). Same-sex pairs born 1977-1984. Intake at target age 11: mean 11.72 (SD 0.43), n=1512, 50.3% female. FU1 at target 14: mean 14.8 (SD 0.53), n=1404. FU4 at target 24: mean 25.29 (SD 0.74), n=1328. 972 MZ (64%) and 540 DZ (36%) twins.

anchors.locator: Methods › Measures › Background Covariate Measures for Propensity Score Estimation Model at Target Age 11, 1st paragraph; Table 1A, rows 1-29
anchors.extracted: Propensity score from 29 intake variables, emphasizing externalizing behaviour: 9 twin-level (IQ, menarche, puberty, GPA, academic problems and motivation, externalizing symptoms, delinquency, conflict with parents) and 20 family-level (sex, age, ethnicity, parent age, IQ, education, occupation, income, family history of externalizing, parental delinquency, psychopathology and alcohol, tobacco and drug use, divorce, a family death). None measures the twin's own tobacco or drug use.

anchors.locator: Methods › Measures › Early Adolescent Alcohol Exposure Measures at Target Age 14, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Two binary self-reports at FU1: ever drank alcohol without parental permission (505 exposed, given as 36%, which is of the 1404 at FU1); ever intoxicated (212, 15%). No difference by zygosity (chi-square 0.192, p=0.66; 0.691, p=0.41). Discordance for early use: MZ pairs 20%, DZ 26%. For intoxication: 9% and 12%.

anchors.locator: Methods › Statistical Analyses › Cotwin Control Application and Exposure Effect Estimation, 1st paragraph (run-in heading; in the PMC markup the 3rd paragraph of 'Propensity Score Estimation, Weighting, and Exposure Effect Estimation')
anchors.extracted: The within-pair (individual-level) coefficient uses only influences not shared by co-twins. It is free of shared environment and of 50% (DZ) or 100% (MZ) of genetic influences. It can be read as causal only if no environmental confounders differ within pairs. GEE was used.

anchors.locator: Results › Propensity Score and Inverse Probability of Treatment Weights, 2nd paragraph; Table 1A, unweighted column
anchors.extracted: Unweighted: 13 of 29 covariates exceeded a standardized difference of 0.25 between twins who had drunk by FU1 and those who had not (19 of 29 for intoxication). Early-use examples: twin delinquent behaviours 0.51, parent tobacco index 0.45, parent alcohol index 0.39, academic motivation -0.38, twin externalizing 0.33, parent delinquency 0.32. After weighting, the mean absolute difference fell from 0.23 to 0.03 (0.29 to 0.07 for intoxication), all below 0.25.

anchors.locator: Results › Propensity Score and Inverse Probability of Treatment Weights, 3rd paragraph; Table 1A, discordant-pair columns
anchors.extracted: Within discordant pairs, all individual-level covariates were balanced (early use: largest was externalizing symptoms, 0.20 all pairs, 0.19 MZ, 0.21 DZ). The only exception was puberty in DZ pairs discordant for intoxication (0.31, Table 1B).

anchors.locator: Table 2A, row 'Alcohol use quantity and frequency index'
anchors.extracted: Early alcohol use, standardized beta (SE): unweighted 0.63 (0.06); propensity-weighted 0.57 (0.06); within all discordant pairs 0.21 (0.09); discordant MZ 0.22 (0.10); discordant DZ 0.20 (0.14). Editors' calculation: within-pair/weighted = 0.37 (all) and 0.39 (MZ); two-sided p from beta/SE about 0.020 (all) and 0.028 (MZ).

anchors.locator: Table 2A, row 'Alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms'
anchors.extracted: Early alcohol use: unweighted 0.46 (0.06); weighted 0.36 (0.07); all pairs 0.24 (0.11); MZ 0.17 (0.14); DZ 0.34 (0.16). Editors' calculation for MZ: z = 1.21, two-sided p about 0.22, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.44.

anchors.locator: Table 2B, row 'Alcohol abuse or dependence symptoms'
anchors.extracted: Early intoxication: unweighted 0.53 (0.10); weighted 0.31 (0.11); all pairs 0.29 (0.15), z = 1.93, two-sided p about 0.053 (editors' calculation); MZ 0.15 (0.19); DZ 0.51 (0.25).

anchors.locator: Results › Estimated Effects of Early Alcohol Exposures on Adult Outcomes, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Within-pair effects of both exposures were attenuated relative to the weighted estimates but stayed significant for substance outcomes, antisocial behaviour and dependent stressful life events. The exception was early intoxication and antisocial behaviour. Zygosity did not significantly moderate any within-pair effect, though several substance measures were significant in DZ but not MZ pairs.

anchors.locator: Tables 2A and 2B, P-value columns; Abstract › Findings
anchors.extracted: The printed p-values match the standard normal density at beta/SE, not two-sided p-values. Examples: 0.00 (SE 0.12) printed 0.396; 0.08 (0.08) printed 0.242, the density at z = 1 (two-sided p 0.32); -0.05 (0.08) printed 0.320 (two-sided p 0.53). The abstract's p = 0.031 for 0.21 (0.09) corresponds to a two-sided p of about 0.020 (editors' calculation).

The authors read the attenuation of within-pair estimates relative to the weighted ones as unmeasured confounding missed by the propensity model. They note that random measurement error in the exposure also shrinks within-pair estimates relative to unpaired ones.
Discordant MZ pairs give the clearest estimate. MZ and DZ estimates did not differ significantly. Higher DZ estimates for several substance outcomes suggest partial confounding by genes in DZ pairs.

Main limitation of co-twin control: it cannot separate causal effects from confounders not shared by exposure-discordant twins. Nearly all measured individual-level predictors were balanced within discordant pairs.

Authors' reading: the analyses support a causal effect of early alcohol use on adult functioning (no social-functioning outcome was associated after weighting). The abstract says early exposures predict adult alcohol problems despite stringent adjustment for measured and unmeasured confounding. Within MZ pairs the abuse or dependence association was not significant.

Conclusion hedged: early use and intoxication may be causally linked to adult alcohol and drug outcomes, antisocial behaviour and dependent stressful life events, but only if there is no unmeasured or non-shared confounding. No reliable effects on social functioning or independence. Further research is needed to know whether the apparent effects are real.

key_findings.correction: The last clause should read: the unweighted associations with interpersonal problems and adult independence lost nominal significance after weighting. Interpersonal problems fell from 0.15 (SE 0.06) to 0.08 (0.08). Adult independence was essentially unchanged, 0.16 (0.07) to 0.15 (0.08), z about 1.9; it lost significance through a larger SE, not a smaller coefficient (for early intoxication 0.18 before and after weighting, Table 2B). 'Disappeared' overstates this.

The authors' reading of larger DZ estimates as partial genetic confounding is in the Discussion's 5th paragraph, not the 4th (8 paragraphs, checked in the page DOM). Results › Estimated Effects, 2nd paragraph, and Tables 2A/2B are correct.
Note: after weighting, the adult-independence estimates are not near zero (early use 0.15, SE 0.08; intoxication 0.18, SE 0.11) and only miss significance. Within pairs they are null (0.00 and 0.01).

Exposure measurement error is in the Discussion's 4th paragraph. The inability to separate causal effects from confounders not shared by co-twins is in the 6th paragraph. The card gives the 3rd and 5th (8 paragraphs, checked in the page DOM).

reporting_issues.note: Found independently in step 1. I recomputed the card's examples and further rows (e.g. -0.05/0.08 printed 0.320 vs two-sided p 0.53; 0.21/0.09 two-sided p 0.0196 vs printed 0.031). The crossover near |z| = 1.6 is right. One printed value, MZ drug classes 0.41 (0.12) p=0.004, fits neither the density (about 0.001-0.002) nor the two-sided p (about 0.0006).

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E some concerns overall, with no domain worse than some concerns. Confounding at some concerns is defensible: propensity weighting plus co-twin control, with the twin's own early substance use and other non-shared factors unaddressed.

interpretation_gap.note: The card's four gaps are all correct, but they add up to 'substantial', not 'minor'. The abstract's Findings say outcomes related to 'social functioning' stayed significant after weighting, but none of the four social-functioning outcomes did. Its Conclusions say early exposures predict adult alcohol problems despite stringent adjustment for non-measured confounding, which failed in the cleanest test (MZ 0.17, SE 0.14) and for intoxication in all pairs (0.29, SE 0.15). The Discussion extends causal language to 'adult functioning'. The hedged final paragraph does not reach the abstract. This is a rating difference for the senior author.

missed: Abstract › Findings: after propensity weighting, 'several adult outcomes related to substance use or social functioning' remained significant. In Table 2A none of the four outcomes the Results call social functioning or independence (family relationships, interpersonal problems, social engagement, adult independence) did; only antisocial symptoms and dependent stressful life events, which the Results class separately, did.

Discussion, 2nd paragraph: the authors put the loss of significance for adult independence after weighting down to confounding, but the coefficient hardly changed (0.16 to 0.15; 0.18 to 0.18 for intoxication). The weighting widened the SE rather than removing an association. This affects key finding 2 and the card's 'results_show' sentence ('associations with social functioning and independence disappeared after weighting').
